title: Fetch, Decode, Execute
description: Fetch, Decode, Execute is the 1973 second album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of heavy blues rock that open up the computer and look inside. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Byt plays lead guitar, and Bytes plays drums and sings backup. Logic gates, binary and two’s complement, floating point, flip-flops, registers, the instruction cycle, machine code, the memory hierarchy, interrupts, pipelining and performance, all the way down to the stored-program idea that makes it all work. Recorded inside a mainframe cabinet for the reverb. Bytes found out he’s made of eight flip-flops. Play loud. Fetch, decode, repeat.
tagline: The 1973 heavy blues follow-up from Procedural Byts: a computer architecture course in twelve songs, recorded inside the machine.
lineup: Still a power trio. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Byt plays lead guitar. Bytes plays drums and sings backup.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, and as of this album, she can prove it’s exactly one hex digit. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass, and her solos on this record are about counting: up the neck, around and back to zero.

members.name: Byt
members.bio: One bit, on or off, and never more at home than on an album about logic gates. Byt takes most of the solos, and on this record they show you the machine working: notes that are either on or silent, licks that load and store, a solo that runs down the memory hierarchy.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, and now he knows it literally: eight flip-flops in a row. Bytes plays drums, sings backup and shouts the call-and-response parts, and on this album he finally lets the clock crystal set the tempo.

members.name: Null
members.bio: Sat on the front panel for the whole weekend. Halted the machine once. Has not commented.

story.heading: Recorded Inside the Machine
paragraphs: After CS1, the band wanted to know what was underneath the code. Byt said it was magic. Nyble said it was gates. Null said nothing, which everyone took as a vote for gates. So they decided to record the second album inside the machine to find out.

They booked a weekend in the university’s machine room and set up inside an empty mainframe cabinet, “for the reverb.” The cooling fans are audible on every track. The engineer set the tempo of each song from the computer’s clock crystal, and Bytes refused to follow it, right up until the Flip-Flop sessions, when he learned he is made of eight flip-flops and accepted the clock as his true drummer.
Nyble finally looked up what a nibble is: four bits, half a byte, exactly one hexadecimal digit. She put it in the bridge of Two’s Complement and has been insufferable about it ever since.

Null spent the sessions sitting on the computer’s front panel. During one take of Speak in Opcodes, the duck settled onto the halt switch and stopped the machine dead. The band kept the take. It is the last bar of the bridge.

The cover is a photograph of that front panel. Eight of the lights are lit in the pattern 01001000, which is the letter H in ASCII, the first letter of Hello, World. The band says they meant to photograph the whole word, but the duck sat on the switches.

cover_sub: The second album, 1973. Recorded inside the machine.

songs.title: Logic Gates of Hell

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Two wires come in and only one goes out,
The AND gate opens only when there’s no doubt.
Both must be high or the door stays shut,
One and one is one, and that’s the only cut!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Logic gates of hell! (AND, OR, NOT!)
Every thought you have is a wire running hot!
Ones and zeros flowing through the iron and the shell,
Welcome to the logic gates of hell!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: OR lets you through if either one is true,
NOT inverts the signal, whatever comes through.
Stack them in a circuit, wire them row by row,
Add two numbers up and watch the carry go!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: NAND! (NAND!) The gate that rules them all!
Build any other gate from NAND and watch them fall!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt plays only two kinds of notes: one bent all the way up, or none at all. On or off. Bytes answers on the snare only when Byt and Nyble play at the same moment: an AND gate you can hear.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Logic gates of hell! (AND, OR, NOT!)
Every thought you have is a wire running hot!
Ones and zeros flowing through the iron and the shell,
Welcome to the logic gates of hell!

songs.note: Opens with the sound of the mainframe powering up, recorded for real. The band says the hum is in tune.
songs.lesson: Computers are built from logic gates. AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1, OR when either is, and NOT flips its input. Gates combine into circuits like adders, and NAND alone can build every other gate.

songs.title: Two’s Complement

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Eight little switches in a row upon the wall,
Count them up in binary, from nothing to it all.
Zero up to two fifty-five, every switch a power of two,
But how do you go negative with no minus sign for you?

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Two’s complement! Flip the bits and add one!
Two’s complement! Now the negative’s done!
The top bit tells you if you’re standing tall or low,
Minus one is all ones, baby, now you know!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A hundred twenty-seven is the highest you can climb,
Add one more and you wrap around to minus every time.
Overflow, overflow, the number bites its tail,
The odometer rolls over and the math begins to fail!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Hex! (Hex!) Sixteen at a time!
Four bits make a digit, it’s a Nyble on the line!

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble climbs the neck one fret at a time, counting up, until she runs out of frets and the line wraps around to the lowest note on the bass: overflow.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Two’s complement! Flip the bits and add one!
Two’s complement! Now the negative’s done!
The top bit tells you if you’re standing tall or low,
Minus one is all ones, baby, now you know!

songs.note: Nyble’s favorite, because the bridge is about her.
songs.lesson: Integers are stored in binary, each bit a power of two. Two’s complement stores negatives: flip every bit and add one. The top bit is the sign, an 8-bit signed value runs from −128 to 127, and going past the top wraps around (overflow). Hexadecimal packs four bits into each digit.

songs.title: Floating Point Blues

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Woke up this morning, added point one and point two,
The answer wasn’t point three, Lord, what am I gonna do?
The machine looked me in the eye and said it’s close as I can get,
A little bit of rounding is the deepest kind of debt.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: I got the floating point blues,
Can’t store a tenth exactly, it’s a number I lose,
A sign and an exponent and a mantissa too,
Close enough is all the machine can do!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Some numbers go on forever in the binary sea,
A third in decimal, a tenth in base two, they never let me be.
Big numbers, tiny numbers, the point floats where it may,
But the gaps between them grow the further you go away.

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Never test for equal! (Never test for equal!)
When the numbers float!
Check if they’re close enough, that’s the only antidote!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt plays a slow blues solo where every note is bent just shy of where it should land. Close enough to sound right, never exactly on pitch.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: I got the floating point blues,
Can’t store a tenth exactly, it’s a number I lose,
A sign and an exponent and a mantissa too,
Close enough is all the machine can do!

songs.note: Recorded in one take, which Byt says was close enough.
songs.lesson: Real numbers are stored as floating point: a sign, an exponent and a mantissa. Many decimals, like 0.1, can’t be stored exactly in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 isn’t exactly 0.3. Compare floats with a tolerance instead of `==`. Precision is relative: the gaps between representable numbers grow as numbers get larger.

songs.title: Flip-Flop

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A gate forgets the moment that the current goes away,
But wire two gates in a loop and the bit will stay.
Set it and it holds, reset it and it’s gone,
One bit of memory, holding on and on!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Flip-flop! Hold that bit!
Flip-flop! Don’t let go of it!
Wait for the clock to tick and then you change your mind,
Flip-flop, flip-flop, one bit at a time!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Eight of us together and you’ve got yourself a byte,
Lined up in a register, holding on tight.
The clock is the drummer and it tells us when to move,
Every tick we flip or flop, locked into the groove!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Combinational! (Forgets!) Sequential! (Remembers!)
State is the fire that survives the embers!

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays the clock. Every hi-hat tick is a clock edge, and the band only changes chords on the tick, never between. Then he plays eight separate hits across eight drums: one byte.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Flip-flop! Hold that bit!
Flip-flop! Don’t let go of it!
Wait for the clock to tick and then you change your mind,
Flip-flop, flip-flop, one bit at a time!

songs.note: Bytes learned during these sessions that he is made of eight flip-flops. He took it surprisingly well.
songs.lesson: Gates alone have no memory. Wiring gates in a feedback loop makes latches and flip-flops, which each store one bit. A clock signal decides when stored values change. Eight flip-flops make a byte, and groups of them form registers.

songs.title: Register Blues

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Up close to the fire where the ALU burns,
Live the registers, waiting for their turns.
The fastest memory in the whole machine,
But only a handful, the fewest you’ve seen.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: I got the register blues,
Only a few of us, so be careful what you choose,
Load it in and add it up and store it back away,
The ALU is cooking and it cooks it every day!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The ALU adds, subtracts, compares and shifts,
Takes two registers and gives the answer a lift.
The accumulator holds the running sum,
The flags say zero, carry, sign, when the work is done!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Load! (Load!) Add! (Add!) Store! (Store!)
Move it from the memory and back out the door!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt is allowed only four licks, one per register. He loads one, adds another to it, and stores the result back, building the whole solo out of four tiny phrases.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: I got the register blues,
Only a few of us, so be careful what you choose,
Load it in and add it up and store it back away,
The ALU is cooking and it cooks it every day!

songs.note: The shortest lyric sheet on the album. There are only so many registers.
songs.lesson: Registers are a handful of very fast storage locations inside the CPU. The ALU (arithmetic logic unit) does arithmetic and logic on register values and sets status flags like zero, carry and sign. Most work follows the same pattern: load, compute, store.

songs.title: Fetch, Decode, Execute

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: In the heart of the machine there is a counter…
And it only knows one word: next.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The program counter points to where the next instruction lies,
Fetch it from the memory and bring it up inside.
Decode the bits to find out what it wants to do,
Execute the order, then the counter moves on through!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Fetch! Decode! Execute!
Round and round, it’s absolute!
A million times a second, never stopping, never mute,
Fetch! Decode! Execute!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: An add, a load, a jump to somewhere new,
The counter changes and the program follows through.
Branch if it’s zero, loop back to the start,
That’s every if and while you wrote, beating in the heart!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Every loop you ever wrote! (Is a jump!)
Every if you ever wrote! (Is a branch!)
Down below the code you know, the machine is at work,
One instruction at a time, in the dark!

parts.label: Instrumental break: full band
parts.desc: The band plays a three-part riff over and over: Byt fetches, Nyble decodes, Bytes executes. Each cycle is a little faster, until the riff is a blur and the counter never stops.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Fetch! Decode! Execute!
Round and round, it’s absolute!
A million times a second, never stopping, never mute,
Fetch! Decode! Execute!

songs.note: The title track. The riff has three parts and never stops cycling, which is the point.
songs.lesson: The CPU repeats the instruction cycle forever: fetch the instruction at the address in the program counter, decode it, execute it, and move the counter on. Jumps and branches change the program counter, which is how loops and if statements work underneath.

songs.title: Speak in Opcodes

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The machine doesn’t speak your language, it doesn’t know your words,
Underneath it’s numbers, the only tongue it’s heard.
Every instruction is an opcode and a place,
Assembly gives it names so we can look it in the face!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Speak in opcodes! (Load! Add! Jump!)
Speak in opcodes! Feel the machine pump!
The compiler turns your verses into numbers in a row,
Speak in opcodes, it’s the only way to go!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The instruction set’s a contract, every chip has its own,
Move this, compare that, every opcode carved in stone.
The assembler turns the names to numbers, one for one,
And the numbers hit the wires, and the work is done!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Move! (Move it!) Compare! (Compare it!)
Jump! (Jump it!) Halt! (Halt!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble’s solo is pure rhythm, and each pattern stands for one opcode: long-short-short is load, short-long is add, three hits is jump. By the end, the band can follow a whole program without a single word.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Speak in opcodes! (Load! Add! Jump!)
Speak in opcodes! Feel the machine pump!
The compiler turns your verses into numbers in a row,
Speak in opcodes, it’s the only way to go!

songs.note: The last bar of the bridge is real. Null sat on the halt switch on the front panel and stopped the machine mid-take.
songs.lesson: Machine code is binary instructions: an opcode (the operation) plus operands (registers or addresses). Each processor family has its own instruction set. Assembly language gives opcodes readable names, an assembler translates them one for one, and compilers translate high-level code down to these instructions.

songs.title: The Memory Hierarchy

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: At the top, the registers, fast and very few,
Then the cache, then the main memory, waiting just for you.
Down below, the disk drive spins, a giant slow and wide,
Every step is bigger, but it’s slower down inside.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Down the memory hierarchy!
Faster at the top, but smaller, you see!
Bigger as you go down, but you wait and wait,
Keep what you need up high, or you’ll be late!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Locality, locality, the secret of the speed,
Use it once, you’ll use it soon, and what’s next door you’ll need.
Time and space, the cache keeps what you touched before,
A hit is like the lightning, but a miss goes to the floor!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Cache hit! (Fast!) Cache miss! (Slow!)
Walk the array in order and watch the cache glow!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt starts at the very top of the neck, blindingly fast, and works his way down. Every octave lower, the notes get heavier and slower, until the solo ends on one long low note that takes forever to arrive: the disk.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Down the memory hierarchy!
Faster at the top, but smaller, you see!
Bigger as you go down, but you wait and wait,
Keep what you need up high, or you’ll be late!

songs.note: The longest song on the album. It gets slower every verse, on purpose.
songs.lesson: Memory is a hierarchy: registers, cache, main memory and disk, each level bigger, cheaper and slower than the one above. Caches work because of locality: recently used data tends to be used again (temporal), and nearby data tends to be used soon (spatial). Hits are fast, misses fall through to slower levels, and walking data in order is cache-friendly.

songs.title: Interrupt

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I’m running through the program, I’m deep inside the track,
When the keyboard sends a signal and it stops me in my tracks!
Save where I was, the registers and all,
Jump to the handler and answer the call!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Interrupt! (Stop!) Something needs you now!
Interrupt! (Stop!) Take a break somehow!
Save it all and handle it, and then you come right back,
Pick up the program right where you left the track!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The printer’s ready now, the disk has found the file,
The clock says that your time is up, you’ve been running for a while.
No need to keep on asking, no checking every beat,
The device will tap your shoulder when the work is complete!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Polling! (Are you done? Are you done? Are you done?)
Interrupts! (I’ll tell you when I’m done!)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes keeps a steady groove, and every time Byt hits a sudden chord, Bytes stops, plays a short fill to handle it, then drops back into the groove exactly where he left off.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Interrupt! (Stop!) Something needs you now!
Interrupt! (Stop!) Take a break somehow!
Save it all and handle it, and then you come right back,
Pick up the program right where you left the track!

songs.note: The engineer kept ringing a phone in the control room during the take. The band decided that was the song.
songs.lesson: Input and output devices get the CPU’s attention with interrupts. The CPU saves its state, runs an interrupt handler, then restores its state and carries on. Interrupts beat polling, which means checking a device over and over, and timer interrupts let an operating system switch between programs.

songs.title: Pipeline

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: One instruction at a time is a lonely way to go,
Fetch, decode, execute, and everyone waits in a row.
But build a line of workers and give each one a stage,
Five instructions in the pipeline, all of them engaged!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Pipeline! Overlap the work!
Pipeline! Every stage goes berserk!
One finishes every cycle when the pipe is full,
Pipeline, pipeline, the iron push and pull!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: But the next one needs the answer that the last one hasn’t made,
A hazard in the pipeline and the whole line is delayed.
A branch that goes the wrong way, flush it all away,
Predict which way it’s going and you’ll save the day!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Stall! (Stall!) A bubble in the line!
Forward the answer and you’ll still be on time!

parts.label: Instrumental break: full band
parts.desc: The band plays the same riff as a round: Bytes starts, Nyble comes in a bar later, Byt a bar after that. When Byt takes a wrong branch, everyone stops, flushes, and comes back in.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Pipeline! Overlap the work!
Pipeline! Every stage goes berserk!
One finishes every cycle when the pipe is full,
Pipeline, pipeline, the iron push and pull!

songs.note: Played as a round, so every bar has three parts of the riff happening at once.
songs.lesson: Pipelining overlaps the stages of different instructions, so a new instruction can start every cycle and throughput goes up. A data hazard (needing a result that isn’t finished) causes a stall or is solved by forwarding. Branches cause control hazards, which branch prediction reduces.

songs.title: Clock Speed

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Tick goes the crystal, a million times a second,
Every tick a step, that’s how the speed is reckoned.
But some instructions take one tick and some take ten,
Count the cycles per instruction, then count them again!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Clock speed! Faster every year!
Clock speed! But it isn’t all that’s here!
Instructions times the cycles times the tick,
Better code and better chips, that’s the only trick!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Double up the clock and the heat begins to rise,
Do more in every tick, that’s the way to win the prize.
Benchmark it and measure it, don’t believe the hype,
The fastest chip on paper can still be the slowest type!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Speed up one part! (By how much?)
Only as much as it’s used! (That’s the crutch!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt starts the solo slow, doubles the speed, then doubles it again. Somewhere past the third doubling his amp starts to smoke, and he has to play smarter instead of faster.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Clock speed! Faster every year!
Clock speed! But it isn’t all that’s here!
Instructions times the cycles times the tick,
Better code and better chips, that’s the only trick!

songs.note: Byt’s amp really did start smoking during the solo. It’s still on the tape.
songs.lesson: CPU time equals instruction count × cycles per instruction × clock cycle time. A faster clock adds heat and power, so doing more work per cycle matters too. Measure with benchmarks, not specs. Amdahl’s law: speeding up one part helps only as much as that part is used.

songs.title: Stored Program

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: Once, you programmed a machine by rewiring it.
Then someone had a better idea.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: They used to wire the program, cables plugged by hand,
Change the job and change the wires, a whole new circuit planned.
Then the program went in memory, right beside the data there,
Numbers that are instructions, numbers everywhere!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Stored program! Instructions in the store!
Stored program! Data and code, and nothing more!
The same memory holds the song and the singer too,
Load a new program and the machine is someone new!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Your words become the opcodes, the opcodes become the bits,
The bits become the voltage, and the gates decide what fits.
From Hello, World at the top down to the silicon sand,
It’s layers upon layers, and the machine is in your hand!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Abstraction! (Layer by layer!)
Code to assembly, to gates, to the wire!

parts.label: Instrumental break: full band
parts.desc: The whole band plays the album backwards, layer by layer: a riff from the title track, the opcode rhythm, the flip-flop clock, and finally the slow gate riff from the first song. From the program all the way down to the gates.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Stored program! Instructions in the store!
Stored program! Data and code, and nothing more!
The same memory holds the song and the singer too,
Load a new program and the machine is someone new!

songs.note: The closer runs the album backwards, from the program down to the gates.
songs.lesson: In the stored-program design, instructions and data live in the same memory, so a computer can run any program just by loading it. Computing is layers of abstraction: high-level code, assembly, machine code, logic gates and transistors.
